newsitem.title: TAIWAN: YEAREND-Taiwan oil utility suffers tumultuous year.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Taiwan oil utility suffers tumultuous year.

text.p: The "Year of the Rat" is supposed to be a prosperous and industrious one under the Chinese horoscope, but 1996 was not a good year for Taiwan's state oil monopoly.

Chinese Petroleum Corp's nightmarish year saw more than a dozen major accidents -- including fires, explosions and spills -- that led to costly shutdowns, delays and more than T$120 million in compensation claims and fines.
The company's president resigned after the accidents sparked criticism from parliament and public anger.
"We have more than 100 factories and it's impossible that there are absolutely no accidents," new president Pan Wen-yen said when he took the office in late November.
"We will try our best to cut down the number of accidents," Pan said. "But even airplanes fall from the sky. The society should give us time to improve."
Since Pan took office, no accident has been reported.

But less than two weeks before the end of the tumultuous year, Chinese Petroleum's chairman was indicted on charges of improprieties during his tenure as mayor of Taiwan's central Taichung city several years ago.
Chang Tzu-yuan was indicted on charges stemming from allegations of misconduct in Taichung city government's rezoning of local property.
Though Chang denied the charges, he was replaced by vice economics minister Lee Shu-jeou.

Regardless of whether Chang's removal ends the oil giant's troubles, the company has vowed to upgrade its competitiveness and conduct reforms by completing its long-awaited privatisation on schedule by July 2000.

The island's only oil producer is bracing for competition as early as 1999 with the upcoming liberalisation of the refined oil products market, but analysts doubted the ability of a monopoly to improve.

"It's impossible that Chinese Petroleum can conduct internal reforms itself if it remains as a state monopoly," said economist Wu Hui-ling at the independent Chung-hua Institute for Economic Research.

The Energy Commission in June removed barriers to private oil imports, but the market is in effect closed until 1999, when Chinese Petroleum's only would-be rival, Formosa Plastics, opens a refinery at its new US$9 billion petrochemical complex.
A qualifying clause in the new rules limits import volume to less than 50 percent of an importer's annual oil production, meaning firms with no production capability are ineligible to import.
"There will be another oil producer, but the competition is still not strong enough to force it to face its existing problems," Wu said, noting bureaucracy in the state firm.
Chinese Petroleum was likely to maintain its monopoly status even after 1999, Wu said.

Under Chinese Petroleum's privatisation programme, 15 percent of the company's equity would be released in the first year to the local stock market to establish a market price for subsequent stock swaps with foreign oil companies.
"The stock swaps are intended to secure Taiwan's oil supply," vice president Roy Chiu said. "Any firm holding major oil reserves is a likely candidate for a swap."
Chinese Petroleum adopts a July/June fiscal year system.
The process will be completed in 1999-2000 when more than 50 percent of the company falls into private hands.

The oil monopoly reported an unaudited net profit of T$17.6 billion in 1995/96, compared with an audited T$14.3 billion net profit in 1994/95. That marked it as one of the most money-making companies on the island.

However, the state utility, with a book value of over T$350 billion and T$230 billion in net assets, has started to report huge budget deficits, with a pre-tax loss of T$1.129 billion in November, and company officials blamed the deficit on parliament's objection to the firm's proposal to hike domestic oil prices.

The budget stalemate in parliament and popular opposition have prevented Chinese Petroleum from carrying through oil price increases that would enable it to balance its budget at a time when world oil prices are sharply higher than it had anticipated.
Chinese Petroleum's November oil import costs averaged US$22.13 per barrel, much higher than the budgeted US$15.26 per barrel, according to company figures.
The oil monopoly imported 12.8 million barrels in November, bringing the cumulative total since the start of the fiscal year on July 1 to 91.7 million barrels, the figures showed.
In addition to the huge deficits, the company's long-term ambition to internationalise its operations was depressed.
It had put 12 of its 18 major overseas projects on hold, reflecting a government policy earlier this year to bolster state-sector investment in Taiwan to ensure a local economic recovery.
Parliament has cut the monopoly's budget for key overseas expansion programmes in Indonesia and Vietnam.

"If there is no strong competition at home, it's hard for Chinese Petroleum to improve its structure and operations no matter how many executives step down or how many overseas projects it will have," Wu said.
"The only solution is to allow a completely free oil market and that will stimulate the company," Wu said.
